verses.text: “Dominion and fear are with him. He makes peace in his high places.
Can his armies be counted? On whom does his light not arise?
How then can man be just with God? Or how can he who is born of a woman be clean?
Behold, even the moon has no brightness, and the stars are not pure in his sight;
How much less man, who is a worm, the son of man, who is a worm!”

footnotes.content: Bildad rises to speak, and we can feel the weariness in the room. His friends have been talking in circles, and he knows it. Yet he must try once more to help Job see what he cannot.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Dominion and fear" — Bildad is describing the sovereignty of the Almighty, painting a picture of a God who commands both power and awe. He speaks truly: all authority rests with Him, and His peace is absolute. Yet he speaks as if Job has forgotten this, as if understanding it were enough to heal a breaking heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bildad points to God's unnumbered armies and the light that reaches every corner—a picture of God's immense power and presence. But Job already knows God is powerful. What Job questions is whether that power is turned toward him in love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here Bildad reaches for the heart of the matter: How can sinful humanity stand righteous before a holy God? This question is profound and true. But it assumes Job's suffering is the price of his own uncleanness—a conclusion that misses the mystery of Job's faithfulness and the grace that meets us in our weakness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even the moon loses its light, even the stars are dim in God's sight. Bildad is humbling himself, declaring that all creation falls short of God's purity. This is a true confession—yet it ends in despair rather than in the hope that God's holiness is not meant to crush us, but to call us home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bildad calls man a worm—and in that image lies an old echo. Readers today hear an echo: we too are small and finite before God's greatness. Yet we also know something Bildad seems to have lost sight of—that God bent down to embrace what is broken, to walk among the worms and call them beloved. A worm, yes; but never unloved.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
